highlights.title: Highlights
highlights.description:
Conway's refinement conjecture [Con76, p. 46] says: if $ab=cd$ for omnific integers, then $a=ef$, $b=gh$, $c=eg$, $d=fh$ for some omnific integers $e,f,g,h$.

We use the vocabulary of [LM24, §2.5]. An element $b$ of an integral domain is primal if whenever $b$ divides $cd$ there are $b_1,b_2$ with $b=b_1b_2$, $b_1\mid c$ and $b_2\mid d$. A domain has the refinement property if $bc=de$ implies $b=fg$, $c=hi$, $d=fh$, $e=gi$ for some $f,g,h,i$; it has this property exactly when every element is primal, and it is then called pre-Schreier [Zaf87]. A GCD domain is a domain in which any two elements have a greatest common divisor; GCD domains are pre-Schreier [LM24, Fact 2.5.1].

Conway normal form identifies the omnific integers with the ring $\mathbb Z+\mathbb R((\mathbf{No}^{<0}))_\kappa$ of series in $t=\omega^{-1}$ with real coefficients, exponents in $\mathbf{No}^{\le0}$, integer constant coefficient, and support of cardinality less than $\kappa$. Here $\mathbf{No}$ is the field of surreal numbers of a Grothendieck universe and $\kappa$ is the cardinality of that universe (Chapter 4). The guide proves that every element of this ring is primal. It proves the same for $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ under conditions on $G$ that include (A1)--(A3) of [LM24, Thm. 9.0.1].

Germs (Chapter 1). Let $K$ be a field and $G$ a nontrivial ordered abelian group that is Cauchy complete for the uniformity of its order topology. Let $J$ be the ideal of series in $K((G^{\le0}))$ whose support is bounded away from $0$. For $b\in K((G^{\le0}))$ and $\gamma\in G$, let $b_{|\gamma}$ be the truncation of $b$ at $\gamma$, the sum of its terms with exponent at most $\gamma$. The germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is the class of $t^{-\gamma}b_{|\gamma}$ modulo $J$ [Ber00, Def. 6.1]. The main statement of Chapter 1 is the convolution formula for the germs of a product; for $G=\mathbb R$ it is [Ber00, Lem. 7.5]. Inductions use the Cantor--Bendixson rank of $0$ in the closure of the support, which drops along the germs just below $0$.

Transcendence (Chapter 2). Let $K$ have characteristic $0$, and let $S$ be a subalgebra of $K((G^{\le0}))/J$ that is a domain and whose elements are classes of series all of whose germs lie in $S$. If a series has its germs at negative exponents in $S$ but its own class is not in $S$, then that class is transcendental over $S$. This transcendence lemma is the main statement of Chapter 2. By Zorn's lemma it follows that $K((G^{\le0}))/J$ is a polynomial ring over $K$. So $J$ is prime; for $G=\mathbb R$ this is [Ber00, Cor. 9.8]. The same method shows that $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ is a polynomial ring over its subring of series with finite support, and hence that $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ is a GCD domain.

Reduction along Archimedean classes (Chapter 3). Grouping exponents along a convex subgroup gives a $D+M$ construction, and primality reduces to two smaller problems; this reduction is the main statement of Chapter 3. At the leading Archimedean class the exponents become real, and the GCD theorem applies. At a limit of classes, primality of germs and an induction on the order type of the set of classes finish the proof.

Surreal exponents (Chapter 4). Conway's construction of a number between two small sets gives the cofinality and completeness conditions. Conway normal form takes the result back to the omnific integers.

phases.title: Germs of translated truncations
phases.description:
This chapter proves the facts about germs that the next chapter uses. The germs of $b^{|\gamma}$ are the germs of $b$ shifted by $\gamma$. The germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is nonzero exactly when $\gamma$ lies in the closed support of $b$, and it is a constant exactly when the germs of $b$ just below $\gamma$ vanish. When $G$ is Cauchy complete, the germ of a product is given by the convolution formula; this is the main statement of the chapter.

Inductions in the next chapter use the Cantor--Bendixson value $V_{\mathrm{CB}}(b)$, defined from the rank of $0$ in the closed support of $b$. It depends only on $[b]$, and only two of its features are used: it vanishes exactly on $J$, and when it is nonzero it drops along the germs of $b$ just below $0$. Compare the ordinal value $v_J$ of [Ber00, Def. 5.2].
phases.setting: $K$ is a field and $G$ a nontrivial ordered abelian group, with its order topology and the associated group uniformity; $G$ is Cauchy complete if every Cauchy filter on $G$ converges. For $b\in K((G^{\le0}))$ and $\gamma\in G$, $b_{|\gamma}$ is the truncation of $b$ at $\gamma$, the sum of the terms of $b$ with exponent at most $\gamma$, and $b^{|\gamma}=t^{-\gamma}b_{|\gamma}$ is the translated truncation, again an element of $K((G^{\le0}))$ [Ber00, Def. 6.1]. $J$ is the ideal of series whose support is bounded away from $0$, $[b]$ is the class of $b$ in $K((G^{\le0}))/J$, and $K$ is identified with its image there. The germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is $[b^{|\gamma}]$. The closed support of a series is the closure of its support in $G$. For a closed well-ordered set $C\subseteq G$ and $x\in C$, $\operatorname{rk}_C(x)$ is the Cantor--Bendixson rank of $x$ in $C$: the ordinal $r$ with $x\in C^{(r)}\setminus C^{(r+1)}$, where $C^{(r)}$ is the $r$-th derived set of $C$.

phases.title: Polynomial presentations
phases.description:
The main statement is the transcendence lemma. Let $G$ be Cauchy complete and $K$ of characteristic $0$. Let $S$ be a $K$-subalgebra of the ring of germs that is a domain and whose elements are classes of series all of whose germs lie in $S$. If a series has all its germs at negative exponents in $S$ but its own class is not in $S$, then that class is transcendental over $S$. The proof takes a polynomial relation of least degree and applies the germ maps to it. Two lemmas prepare it: such a class satisfies no linear relation over $S$, and two series whose germs are proportional near $0$ have classes that differ by a constant factor.

By Zorn's lemma, a maximal algebraically independent set of such classes generates the ring of germs. So the ring of germs is a polynomial ring over $K$ when $G$ is Cauchy complete, and $J$ is prime. The same holds for series whose support has cardinality less than $\kappa$.

For real exponents, a series has only constant germs exactly when its support is finite. The same method then shows that $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ is a polynomial ring over its subring of series with finite support. That subring is a GCD domain [LM24, Fact 2.5.2], so by Gauss's lemma $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ is a GCD domain too.
phases.setting:
$K$ is a field and $G$ a nontrivial ordered abelian group, with its order topology and the associated group uniformity. Write $A=K((G^{\le0}))$ and $Q=A/J$. The germs of $b\in A$ are the classes $[b^{|\xi}]$, $\xi\in G$. For $a=[b]\in Q$ write $V_{\mathrm{CB}}(a)=V_{\mathrm{CB}}(b)$, which depends only on $a$ (Chapter 1). For a $K$-subalgebra $S\subseteq Q$, $A(S)$ is the set of series all of whose germs lie in $S$; for $E\subseteq A$, $[E]$ is the image of $E$ in $Q$. A $K$-subalgebra $E\subseteq A$ is closed under truncation if $b_{|\eta}\in E$ for all $b\in E$ and $\eta\in G$. $K(G^{\le0})$ is the subring of series with finite support, and $Y$, $Y_i$ denote polynomial indeterminates.

Hypothesis (H): $G$ is Cauchy complete, $S\subseteq Q$ is a $K$-subalgebra with $S\subseteq[A(S)]$, $X\in A$ satisfies $[X^{|\xi}]\in S$ for all $\xi<0$, and $x=[X]$.

The transcendence lemma and the results that use it assume that $K$ has characteristic $0$, and say so; the other results hold in every characteristic.

phases.title: Reduction along Archimedean classes
phases.description:
This chapter proves that every element of $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ is primal under conditions on $G$. Regrouping exponents along a convex subgroup $C$ turns $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ into a $D+M$ construction over $D=Z+R((C^{<0}))_\kappa$. So $x$ is primal if its regrouping $\hat x$ and its restriction $\rho_C(x)$ are primal and, in case $\rho_C(x)=0$, $R((C))_\kappa$ is the fraction field of $D$; this step lemma carries the reduction.

The proof is an induction on the order type of the set of nonzero Archimedean classes met by the support. If the set is finite, take $C$ below the leading class; the regrouped series has real exponents, so it is primal by the GCD theorem of Chapter 2. Otherwise take $C$ below a limit of classes. Then the regrouped series is primal because its germ is primal, by the polynomial presentation of the ring of germs, and because restrictions to the convex subgroups $\Gamma_{\preceq q}$ split off factors whose set of classes has smaller order type.
phases.setting:
$G$ is an ordered abelian group, $R$ a field, $Z\subseteq R$ a subring, and $\kappa>\aleph_0$ a cardinal. $R((G))_\kappa$ is the field of series whose support has cardinality less than $\kappa$, and $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ its subring of series with support in $G^{\le0}$ and constant coefficient in $Z$. For $x\ne0$, $v(x)=\min\operatorname{supp}(x)$, and $v(0)=0$. For a convex subgroup $C$, $\rho_C(x)$ is the restriction of $x$ to $C$, the sum of the terms of $x$ with exponent in $C$.

$[g]$ is the Archimedean class of $g\in G$. Classes are ordered by magnitude: $[g]\prec[h]$ if $n|g|<|h|$ for all $n\ge1$, so $[0]$ is the least class. A series meets the classes of the exponents in its support. The nonzero classes met by $x$ form a set $\mathcal C(x)$, well ordered by $\succ$ as the image of the well-ordered set $\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq G^{\le0}$ under the map $g\mapsto[g]$, which is monotone from $\le$ to $\succeq$ on $G^{\le0}$; $\operatorname{ot}\mathcal C(x)$ is its order type. For a nonzero class $\sigma$, $G_{\prec\sigma}$ and $G_{\preceq\sigma}$ are the convex subgroups of elements of class $\prec\sigma$, respectively $\preceq\sigma$. When $G$ is an ordered vector space over an Archimedean ordered field $F$, $H_\sigma$ is a fixed $F$-linear complement of $G_{\prec\sigma}$ in $G_{\preceq\sigma}$. For a set $T$ of nonzero classes, $G_T=\bigcap_{\sigma\in T}G_{\preceq\sigma}$.

When $G$ is a vector space over a field $F$ and $C$ is a convex $F$-subspace, put $\Gamma=G/C$, $L=R((C))_\kappa$ and $D=Z+R((C^{<0}))_\kappa$. For regular $\kappa$, regrouping exponents along an $F$-linear complement of $C$ sends $x$ to $\hat x\in L((\Gamma^{\le0}))_\kappa$, with constant coefficient $\rho_C(x)$, and identifies $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ with $D+L((\Gamma^{<0}))_\kappa$.

Conditions [LM24, Thm. 9.0.1]: (A1)$_\sigma$: $H_\sigma\simeq\mathbb R$ as ordered groups. (A2)$_\sigma$: $\operatorname{cf}(G_{\prec\sigma})\ge\kappa$, or $G_{\prec\sigma}=\{0\}$ and $R=\operatorname{Frac}(Z)$. (A3): $Z$ is pre-Schreier. Further conditions, for a set $T$ of nonzero classes: (B1)$_T$: $\operatorname{cf}(G_T)\ge\kappa$, or $G_T=\{0\}$ and $R=\operatorname{Frac}(Z)$. (B2)$_T$: $G/G_T$ is Cauchy complete for its order topology and group uniformity.

phases.title: Surreal numbers and omnific integers
phases.description:
This chapter checks the conditions of the general theorem for $G=\mathbf{No}$. Conway's construction of a number between two small sets carries the argument.

Each complement $H_\sigma$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb R$. Conway's construction gives the cofinality conditions. It also fills small cuts, and a cut criterion turns this into Cauchy completeness of the quotients $\mathbf{No}/\mathbf{No}_T$.

So every element of $\mathbb Z+\mathbb R((\mathbf{No}^{<0}))_\kappa$ is primal. Conway normal form identifies this ring with the omnific integers. Hence the omnific integers have the refinement property, and every irreducible omnific integer is prime.
phases.setting: Fix a Grothendieck universe and let $\kappa$ be its cardinality, a strongly inaccessible cardinal, in particular regular and uncountable. $\mathbf{No}$ is the field of surreal numbers of birthday less than $\kappa$, and a subset of $\mathbf{No}$ is small if its cardinality is less than $\kappa$. This is the usual way to treat Conway's proper class $\mathbf{No}$ [Con76] as a set: the sets of [Con76] become small subsets, and the condition ``cofinality $\mathbf{On}$'' of [LM24, Prop. 2.4.4] becomes ``cofinality at least $\kappa$''. $\mathbf{Oz}\subseteq\mathbf{No}$ is the ring of omnific integers, the numbers $x$ with $x=\{x-1\mid x+1\}$. $\mathbf{No}$ is an ordered $\mathbb R$-vector space, and Archimedean classes, $\mathbf{No}_{\prec\sigma}$, $\mathbf{No}_{\preceq\sigma}$, $H_\sigma$ and $\mathbf{No}_T$ are as in the previous chapter, with $G=\mathbf{No}$.
